claim: Saretto (Nov 2005 working paper, precursor of Goyal-Saretto 2009; Jan 1996-Jun 2005, sample ends before 2015; near-the-money single-stock options with 30-60 days to expiry, monthly returns from bid-ask mid-points, unhedged, no trading costs unless stated): with no signal applied, calls returned +3.4% per month on average, puts -3.6% and straddles -0.3%; median returns were negative.
quote: Calls have a positive mean return of 3.4%, respectively, while puts and straddles have a negative average returns of –3.6% and –0.3%.
title: Predictability of Implied Volatility (Saretto)

claim: Saretto (Nov 2005 working paper, precursor of Goyal-Saretto 2009; Jan 1996-Jun 2005, sample ends before 2015; near-the-money single-stock options with 30-60 days to expiry, monthly returns from bid-ask mid-points, unhedged, no trading costs unless stated): the long-short straddle return falls as option maturity lengthens: 12.9% per month for options expiring in 1-2 months, 5.9% for 3-4 months and 3.6% for 6-7 months, all held one month.
title: Predictability of Implied Volatility (Saretto)

claim: Saretto (Nov 2005 working paper, precursor of Goyal-Saretto 2009; Jan 1996-Jun 2005, sample ends before 2015; near-the-money single-stock options with 30-60 days to expiry, monthly returns from bid-ask mid-points, unhedged, no trading costs unless stated): the long-short straddle strategy held to expiry (about 47 days) returned 16.1% at mid-points and 5.5% after costs set at an effective spread of 75% of the quoted spread.
quote: The average return to expiration of the long-short strategy is equal to 16.1% when the returns are computed from mid-point prices and 5.5% when transaction costs are applied
title: Predictability of Implied Volatility (Saretto)

claim: Saretto (Nov 2005 working paper, precursor of Goyal-Saretto 2009; Jan 1996-Jun 2005, sample ends before 2015; near-the-money single-stock options with 30-60 days to expiry, monthly returns from bid-ask mid-points, unhedged, no trading costs unless stated): the signal is a monthly cross-sectional forecast of the change in log implied volatility from current implied volatility and the twelve-month averages of implied and realised volatility; stocks whose implied volatility is below their own twelve-month average are predicted to rise.
quote: average and below its own twelve months moving average, has a higher implied volatility
